product: commentary — no product. Reveals a native-ad scaling playbook: mirror ads, news-article copy, interview-style advertorials.
hook: not in file (hook refers to the ad examples, not the commentary post).
body: Playbook: create a mirror ad so the ICP sees herself; write news article-style copy for max CTR; run an interview-style advertorial where the ICP is interviewed about her discovery; use the advertorial to move the reader from unaware to most aware, then push to an educational sales page and finally the offer page.
idea: Native scales when every touchpoint — ad, advertorial, sales page — looks like editorial content, not advertising.
sequencing: Mirror ad: creative shocks the ICP into self-recognition.
News article-style copy maximizes CTR.
Interview-style advertorial: the ICP is 'interviewed' about her discovery.
Advertorial moves the reader from unaware to most aware.
Reader is pushed to an educational sales page.
Then to the offer page.
formatting: Static image + long primary text, leading to an interview-styled advertorial page; visual details not in file.
why_it_works: Each step borrows credibility from a trusted content shape (news, interview); the reader's ad-defenses never engage because no step looks like an ad.
what_to_steal: The interview-style advertorial for Louise Carter — e.g. an 'interview' with a jewelry buyer about discovering why her skin turned green, ending at LC's waterproof pieces.

product: commentary — no product. Reveals the native ad setup recipe: story-feel, selfie or problem-matching photo, 2,500+ word primary text.
hook: not in file (post is the explanation, not an ad).
body: Native ads work because people feel they are reading a story, not seeing an ad. Setup: a normal selfie or a weird photo that matches the problem being sold against, plus a very long primary text built as a story (2,500 words or more). Ends with 'One warning' (truncated).
idea: Disguise the ad as a story: an ordinary photo plus a very long narrative primary text.
sequencing: Photo that looks organic: a normal selfie or a weird photo matching the problem.
Very long primary text (2,500+ words) written as a story.
Reader feels they are reading a story, not an ad.
A warning follows (post truncated).
formatting: Static image + very long primary text (2,500+ words).
why_it_works: Length signals 'story, not ad'; the reader invests time, and invested time converts to trust.
what_to_steal: The 'weird photo that matches the problem' cue — for LC, an unglamorous close-up of a green-stained neck or a faded $12 necklace next to a 2,500-word story.

product: commentary — no product. Reveals why native ads must land on an advertorial, not a product page.
hook: not in file.
body: A native ad has to lead to an advertorial, not a product page: not everyone reads the full primary text before clicking, so the advertorial must carry the angle for early clickers. It does not have to repeat the exact story (truncated).
idea: The advertorial is the safety net for readers who clicked before finishing the ad's story.
sequencing: Reader clicks the native ad mid-story (many never finish the primary text).
Click lands on an advertorial, not the PDP.
Advertorial carries the same angle forward for early clickers.
It does not need to repeat the exact story (truncated).
formatting: Native static → advertorial (not PDP); visual details not in file.
why_it_works: Click intent is fragile — dumping a mid-story reader on a product page breaks the narrative spell; the advertorial preserves it.
what_to_steal: Angle-carry rule for LC: any native story static must land on an advertorial that continues the same problem angle, never a cold PDP.

product: commentary — no product. Reveals the two-step native ad funnel architecture.
hook: not in file.
body: The native ad funnel start to finish: (1) the ad — a native image plus a long story in the primary text, built for an unaware or problem-aware person; (2) the advertorial — same angle as the ad, keeps the story going, agitates the problem, builds the fear, then brings in the product (truncated).
idea: The ad opens the story for the unaware; the advertorial escalates it and only then introduces the product.
sequencing: Native image + long-story primary text targets unaware/problem-aware readers.
Click goes to an advertorial on the same angle.
Advertorial keeps the story going.
Advertorial agitates the problem and builds fear.
Product is introduced last (post truncated).
formatting: Static image + long primary text → advertorial; visual details not in file.
why_it_works: Unaware audiences cannot be pitched, only storied to; the advertorial does the selling after attention and emotion are banked.
what_to_steal: The two-step LC template: story static ('my necklace turned my neck green before my sister's wedding') → advertorial that agitates (photos, ruined outfits) before revealing LC.

product: commentary — no product. Reveals the news-article/discovery disguise for native statics.
hook: not in file.
body: Native ad hack: make the static look like a news article or discovery piece — e.g. 'Sleep expert reveals why woman over 45…' The product can be hinted at directly in the static or simply shown.
idea: Authority framing ('expert reveals') makes the static read as news, not an ad.
sequencing: Static is styled as a news article or discovery piece.
Headline uses the "expert reveals why…" authority template ("Sleep expert reveals why woman over 45…").
Product is hinted at directly in the static copy…
…or simply shown in the visual.
formatting: Static styled as news article/discovery; visual details not in file.
why_it_works: 'Expert reveals' borrows journalistic authority; readers lower skepticism for news-shaped content.
what_to_steal: LC headline template: 'Jewelry expert reveals why your neck turns green…' as a native static hook.

product: commentary — no product. Reveals five ad formats to test, including camouflage native statics.
hook: not in file (list post).
body: Five formats to test: (1) founder talking head — raw, low production, 30 seconds of genuine talk; (2) voiceless B-roll ads — B-roll + product shots with script as text-overlay bullets; (3) yapper ads — uncut organic talking to camera, feels like a friend; (4) AI educational videos — AI visuals explaining a mechanism, good for health brands; (5) camouflage ads — native-looking image blending into the feed with long-form emotional storytelling from problem to solution to action, so people don't realize it's an ad until invested. Closes noting the format isn't the biggest lever — the angle underneath is (truncated).
idea: Raw, feed-native formats borrow trust from organic content; the angle underneath matters more than the format.
sequencing: Founder talking head: raw, 30s genuine talk.
Voiceless B-roll + text-overlay bullet script.
Yapper: uncut, organic, friend-like.
AI educational: visuals explain the mechanism.
Camouflage static + long-form emotional story; the ad is only recognized once the reader is invested.
formatting: Mixed video/static guidance; camouflage = native-looking static + long-form primary text.
why_it_works: Polish reads as 'advertising'; rawness reads as 'friend' — trust transfers from the format.
what_to_steal: Camouflage statics for LC: organic-looking jewelry photos with long story captions that read as personal posts.

product: commentary — no product. Reveals why before/after photos are the best native ad image.
hook: The before/after image itself — 'a real change, not a product.'
body: People stop scrolling because they see a real change, not a product; change creates curiosity, product shots cause scrolling. The long primary text then tells the full story — what was tried, what failed, what finally worked — with the product entering near the end, after the story has done the emotional work. The click goes to an advertorial on the same angle. Leading with product makes you just another ad; leading with transformation and story gets read to the end before the reader realizes they're being sold to.
idea: Lead with the transformation, not the product — curiosity about the change carries the reader past their ad-defenses.
sequencing: Before/after image stops the scroll via curiosity about the change.
Long primary text opens the struggle story.
Failed attempts build relatability.
Product enters near the end as what finally worked.
Advertorial on the same angle carries the story to the close.
formatting: Before/after static + long primary text → advertorial; two photos attached.
why_it_works: Curiosity gap (what caused the change?) plus narrative transportation — readers finish the story before their skepticism engages.
what_to_steal: Before/after for LC: green-stained skin / faded fast-fashion necklace vs. LC piece after months of daily wear, with the product revealed late in the copy.

Spend scales to six figures a day on the winners.

product: commentary — no product. Reveals an 8-step advertorial structure that outperforms PDPs for Google Shopping traffic.
hook: 'your pdp is not always the best place to send shopping traffic.'
body: Advertorials are presented as an underrated way to scale Google Shopping: they raise conversion and address different buyer psychologies (skeptics, comparison shoppers, objection-heavy buyers). The 8-step structure: open with the problem/transformation sought; explain the hidden mechanism blocking it; introduce the product and how it fixes it; walk through expected outcomes, benefits, and USPs; layer in testimonials, reviews, before/afters; add a comparison chart vs competitors; present offer, guarantee, and CTA; finish with an FAQ handling objections.
idea: Send Shopping traffic to an advertorial, not the PDP — the page pre-sells every objection before the product page.
sequencing: Open with the problem or transformation sought.
Explain the hidden mechanism stopping them.
Introduce the product and how it fixes it.
Walk through outcomes, benefits, USPs.
Layer in testimonials, reviews, before/afters.
Add a comparison chart against competitors.
Present the offer, guarantee, and CTA.
Finish with an objection-handling FAQ.
formatting: Long-form advertorial page; two photos attached.
why_it_works: Shopping traffic is high-intent but comparison-minded; the advertorial answers every objection before the PDP ever loads.
what_to_steal: The full 8-step skeleton for an LC advertorial: 'why your jewelry turns skin green' → LC's PVD process → proof → comparison vs plated jewelry → offer.

idea: Each line of the ad sells the next line — the advertorial, not the ad, does the selling.
sequencing: Illustrated creative stops the scroll.
Long primary text opens the story.

The advertorial closes the sale.

product: commentary — no product. Uses a parasite supplement ad as the example of scroll-stopping static hooks.
hook: 'My sister slept with my husband.'
body: A lesson in static hooks: instead of generic benefit lines ('Support a healthy gut', 'Feel better naturally', 'Cleanse from within'), the ad leads with family betrayal. The product doesn't appear until after the curiosity gap is created; then the twist — 'Because she drains parasites.' It's absurd, creates an information gap, and forces reading the next line. The lesson: people don't stop scrolling because the product is interesting; they stop because they need to know what happens next — then the product inherits that attention.
idea: Open with an absurd, unrelated-sounding story hook; resolve it into the product via a twist line.
sequencing: Shock headline: 'My sister slept with my husband.'
Curiosity gap — the reader must know what happens next.
Twist resolves the story into the product: 'Because she drains parasites.'
Lesson: attention first, product inherits it.
Generic benefit lines shown as the losing alternative.
formatting: Static ad with bold headline text; two photos attached.
why_it_works: Information-gap theory — the brain cannot tolerate an unresolved story, so it keeps reading.
what_to_steal: LC version: 'My bridesmaid ruined my wedding photos' → twist: her $12 necklace turned everyone's neck green — except mine (Louise Carter).

sequencing: Hook: the problem, not the product.
Problem made specific enough for self-recognition.
First-person story of someone else living it.
Payoff: what changed, and the product as… (truncated).

why_it_works: Self-recognition ('that's me') is the strongest scroll-stopper; a third-person story lets the reader observe without feeling sold to.
what_to_steal: The 4-step skeleton as LC's default story-ad template for every native static and yapper script.
